title: ECB President Lagarde warns Europe must build its own AI
excerpt: Lagarde said a sudden loss of access to foreign AI systems could hit every sector of the European economy at once
content_html:
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde warned on Monday that Europe cannot rely solely on imported artificial intelligence from the United States and must develop its own capacity — or risk giving foreign technology suppliers leverage over every corner of its economy.

Speaking in Vienna, Lagarde said AI is different from past imported technologies because a withdrawal of access, or a change in its terms, would reach every sector simultaneously once the technology is embedded in border screening, tax administration, rail dispatch, hospital monitoring, and bank payment systems. "That is leverage of a kind no trade partner has ever held over Europe," she said, "and it could be used in any negotiation, on tariffs or on digital taxes, for example."

Lagarde said Europe's first priority must be expanding its own computing infrastructure. Europe already lacks sufficient data center capacity to meet existing demand, and on current trends that gap is projected to grow more than sixfold within a decade, she said. Closing it could cost as much as €600 billion over ten years, chips included. The E.U.'s new gigafactories are a start, she said, but fill only a fraction of the shortfall, and "Europe needs to build at a different pace altogether."

Beyond infrastructure, Lagarde said Europe must develop AI models competent enough for the majority of use cases and hosted on European systems, so that the prospect of a foreign supplier pulling access no longer constitutes a meaningful threat. She pointed to French firm Mistral as well as a company in San Sebastián that has adapted a Chinese open model to score higher on independent benchmarks than any other European model.

She also argued that European savers are already exposed to the costs of the global AI boom without fully sharing in its gains. Euro area households hold roughly €440 billion in U.S. technology firms, and U.S. hyperscalers issued more than $100 billion in bonds last year, pushing up borrowing costs globally. ECB estimates suggest that if AI is adopted quickly, it could raise productivity by as much as 4% over a decade — an outcome Lagarde called transformative for public finances.

Europe's AI buildout demands a different kind of financing than the bloc currently relies on, Lagarde said. New models and sovereign technology links cannot be funded with debt alone and require patient equity investors prepared to back firms across the years it takes to reach profitability. European households save roughly €1.4 trillion a year, she said, but the markets to channel that capital into homegrown technology do not yet exist at the necessary scale. "Europe must first be able to deploy its savings at home," she said.
